## Preface {.unnumbered}

Having validated the automated HVR pipeline in Chapter 4,
this chapter applies it at population scale to characterize
the HVR's distributional properties, to evaluate its
self-normalizing behavior with respect to head size, and to
establish sex-specific normative aging curves. A key
motivation is the long-standing inconsistency in reported
sex differences in hippocampal volume, which arise from the
choice of head-size correction method. The UK Biobank
provides the large, demographically diverse sample of
cognitively intact subjects needed to systematically
compare correction approaches and to
construct normative centile models using generalized additive
models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS). The
sex-specific normative curves developed here are
subsequently used to analyze the ADNI clinical cohort in
Chapter 6, enabling individualized z-scoring of hippocampal
structure in a disease-enriched population.

The following manuscript has been submitted to
*Human Brain Mapping* (Manuscript ID: XXXX).

\clearpage

## Hippocampal-to-Ventricle Ratio as a Head-Size-Independent Biomarker: Sex Differences and Cognitive Associations in 27,680 UK Biobank Participants {.unnumbered}

Sofía Fernández-Lozano, D. Louis Collins

\vspace{1em}

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Hippocampal volume is a key biomarker for Alzheimer's disease and
brain aging, yet reported sex differences vary substantially
depending on head-size adjustment methods. We examined whether the
hippocampal-to-ventricle ratio (HVR), a self-normalizing measure,
provides more consistent sex difference estimates than conventional
adjustment approaches. Using a subset of UK Biobank structural MRI
data (N = 27,680; 56% female; ages 45--82), we compared sex
differences across four adjustment methods (unadjusted,
proportions, stereotaxic, residualized) and in samples matched on
age and on intracranial volume (ICV). Hippocampal sex differences
reversed direction across methods, ranging from Cohen's $d = -0.89$ (males
larger, unadjusted) to $d = 0.58$ (females larger, proportions),
with a range of 1.5 standard deviations across analytical choices.
In contrast, HVR showed a consistent female advantage ($d = 0.52$)
that persisted in the ICV-matched subsample ($d = 0.19$), confirming
this effect is not a head-size artifact. Males exhibited steeper
cross-sectional age-related HVR differences ($1.7\times$ female rate,
$p < 10^{-50}$), consistent with males showing ventricular expansion at younger
ages. Structural equation modeling revealed that HVR predicted
general cognition comparably to hippocampal volume
($\beta = 0.04$, overlapping CIs), and unlike residualized
hippocampal volume, HVR maintained significant brain-cognition
associations in both sexes. We provide sex-specific normative
centile curves for clinical application. These findings indicate
that previously reported hippocampal sex differences largely reflect
methodological choices rather than biology, while HVR captures
consistent morphological variation related to brain aging that may
have clinical utility.

\vspace{1em}

## Introduction

The hippocampus (HC) is a brain structure used as an early
biomarker for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and brain aging
[@jack_prediction_1999; @jack_hypothetical_2010;
@raz_regional_2005]. Sex differences in brain structures have
been documented, but their interpretation is controversial
[@ritchie_sex_2018; @ruigrok_meta-analysis_2014], largely because
findings depend on whether and how head-size adjustments are
applied [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020;
@nordenskjold_intracranial_2015]. Males have approximately 12%
larger intracranial volume (ICV) than females
[@ruigrok_meta-analysis_2014], and after head-size correction, sex
classification from brain features drops from >80% to
approximately 60% [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020]. This
methodological sensitivity suggests some reported sex differences
may be artifacts of adjustment methods.

Hippocampal atrophy rates predict conversion from mild cognitive
impairment to dementia [@rajagopal_estimating_2024], making
accurate volume assessment clinically consequential. However, males
and females show different rates of age-related brain volume
change, with steeper subcortical volume declines in males across
multiple structures [@ritchie_sex_2018]. These sex-differential
trajectories mean that normative reference values must be
sex-stratified to avoid misclassifying normal variation as
pathological; recent large-scale brain charting efforts have
adopted sex-specific centile modeling for this reason
[@coupe_lifespan_2019; @bethlehem_brain_2022;
@ge_normative_2024].

Multiple adjustment methods exist, each with different
assumptions: proportions (V/ICV) assumes perfect allometric
scaling, residualization (V $-$ $\beta \times$ ICV) removes linear
ICV association, and stereotaxic normalization applies spatial
transformation to a template. These methods can yield
contradictory conclusions about the same brain regions
[@wang_comparison_2024]. For hippocampus, reported sex differences
range from males larger (unadjusted; @ruigrok_meta-analysis_2014)
to females larger (proportions; @sanchis-segura_effects_2020) to
no difference (residualized; @obrien_statistical_2011). The
proportions method can produce biologically implausible results,
while residualization yields more consistent estimates
[@wang_comparison_2024]. No consensus exists on the correct method,
and conclusions depend on analytical choices.

The hippocampal-to-ventricle ratio (HVR), defined as HC / (HC +
LV) where HC denotes total hippocampal volume and LV denotes the
volume of the temporal horns of the lateral ventricles, offers a
potential solution. Both structures scale with head size, making
their ratio self-normalizing. HVR captures the relationship
between hippocampal and ventricular volumes, which show opposite
patterns with age---smaller hippocampus and larger ventricles.
Schoemaker and colleagues introduced HVR and showed that it
provides stronger associations with age and memory than standard
hippocampal volume in healthy aging
[@schoemaker2019]. Subsequent work shows
HVR provides higher effect sizes for distinguishing AD from
controls compared to HC alone
[@fernandez-lozano_enhanced_2025]. However, properties of HVR in
healthy populations and across adjustment methods remain
unexplored.

Age-related ventricular expansion reflects concurrent loss of
surrounding gray and white matter tissue
[@madsen_mapping_2015], and this expansion occurs earlier in males,
with abnormal enlargement appearing in the seventies and
preferentially affecting the frontal horns
[@curra_ventricular_2019]. These sex-differential ventricular
trajectories suggest that a ratio incorporating both hippocampal
and ventricular volumes may capture sex differences in brain aging
that regional tissue volumes miss. Furthermore, brain
structure--cognition associations themselves may differ by sex:
grey matter volumes predict cognitive profiles with different
strength and spatial specificity in older males versus females
[@jockwitz_differential_2024], and hippocampal volume predicts
associative memory in older women but not men
[@zheng_sex_2017]. Whether HVR shows similar sex-differential
cognitive associations remains unknown.

We addressed three questions: (1) Do hippocampal sex differences
vary across head-size adjustment methods while HVR remains
consistent? (2) Do cross-sectional age patterns differ by sex, and
do these patterns differ between HC and HVR depending on
normalization method? (3) Does HVR show comparable cognitive
associations to conventionally adjusted hippocampal volumes?

## Materials and Methods

### Data Source and Participants

Data were obtained from UK Biobank (Application 45551)
[@sudlow_uk_2015; @miller_multimodal_2016]. The initial imaging
sample comprised approximately
`r format(n_initial_imaging, big.mark=",")` participants with
T1-weighted structural MRI. After exclusions (detailed below), the
final analytic sample included
N = `r format(n_primary, big.mark=",")` cognitively intact
participants aged
`r age_min` to `r age_max` years. With this sample size, we had
>99% power to detect small effects (d = 0.10) and >80% power to
detect very small effects (d = 0.05) for two-group comparisons at
$\alpha$ = .05.

Three additional subsamples were defined for specific analyses
(@fig-prisma; @tbl-demographics). The **England subsample**
(N = `r format(n_england, big.mark=",")`) comprised participants
assessed at UK Biobank centres in England and was used for SEM
analyses requiring the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMDP), which
is not comparable across UK countries. This subsample provides
adequate power for detecting standardized path coefficients
$\geq$ 0.02. The **ICV-matched subsample**
(N = `r format(n_matched_pairs * 2, big.mark=",")`) comprised
female--male pairs matched on age ($\pm 1$ year) and ICV
($\pm 25$ cc) drawn from the primary sample, and was used to
isolate sex effects from head-size confounding (see Sex
Differences Across Adjustment Methods). The
**longitudinal subsample** (N = 2,935) comprised participants from
the primary sample who also had a follow-up imaging session
(ses-3), with a mean intersession interval of 2.7 years
(SD = 1.1; range: 1.5--5.0). This subsample was used as a
sensitivity check for normative model calibration (see
Age-Related Patterns and Normative Modeling).

#### Exclusion Criteria

Participants were excluded if they had any of the following ICD-10
diagnoses recorded in linked hospital records: F00-F99 (mental and
behavioral disorders including dementia, mood disorders,
schizophrenia, and anxiety disorders, which are associated with
hippocampal volume alterations [@schmaal_subcortical_2016;
@cao_volumes_2023; @brosch_reduced_2022]); G00-G99 (neurological
diseases including Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis,
epilepsy, and cerebrovascular disease, which directly affect brain
structure [@van_erp_subcortical_2016; @xu_longitudinal_2020;
@koenig2014; @tai_detection_2025]); and Q00-Q07
(congenital CNS malformations affecting normal brain development).
This exclusion strategy selected a sample of cognitively healthy
adults without conditions known to affect hippocampal morphometry.
The full exclusion flow is shown in @fig-prisma.

#### Quality Control

Image segmentations underwent quality control in three stages:
(1) automated quality scores from deep learning-based assessments,
requiring DARQ score $\geq$ 0.25 [@fonov2022darq] and
AssemblyNet rating of "A" (highest quality grade)
[@coupe_assemblynet_2020], (2) statistical outlier detection
excluding participants with age- and head-size-adjusted volumes
exceeding $\pm 3$ SD from the sample mean, and (3) visual
inspection of flagged cases by trained raters for evident
segmentation failures, motion artifacts, or anatomical anomalies.
This multi-stage pipeline is intentionally conservative: in a
large population-based study where statistical power is not a
limiting factor, prioritizing data quality over sample retention
reduces the risk of segmentation errors biasing volumetric
estimates, particularly for small structures like the hippocampus
and temporal horn ventricles where even minor segmentation
failures can produce large relative errors.

For participants with multiple imaging sessions, QC filtering was
applied first, then one session per participant was selected for
cross-sectional analyses. When a participant's baseline session
(ses-2) failed QC but the follow-up session (ses-3) passed, the
follow-up session was retained in the cross-sectional sample.
Longitudinal analyses required both sessions to pass QC.

### Brain Measures

#### Image Acquisition

Images were acquired on Siemens Skyra 3T scanners at three UK
sites (Cheadle, Newcastle, Reading) using a T1-weighted MPRAGE
sequence at 1mm isotropic resolution. Full protocol details are
provided in @alfaro-almagro_image_2018.

#### Segmentation

Hippocampal and ventricular volumes were segmented using an
in-house convolutional neural network trained on manually labeled
data. Validation against manual segmentations showed Dice
$\kappa$ = 0.94 and Pearson r = 0.99
[@fernandez-lozano_enhanced_2025]. Outputs included bilateral
hippocampal volumes (left, right, total) and temporal horn volumes
of the lateral ventricles (left, right, total). Intracranial volume (ICV) was
obtained from AssemblyNet [@coupe_assemblynet_2020], a
large-ensemble convolutional neural network for whole-brain MRI
segmentation.

#### Head-Size Adjustment Methods

Four adjustment approaches were applied to hippocampal and
ventricular volumes [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020;
@sanfilipo_correction_2004]:

1. **Unadjusted**: raw volumes in native space (mL), which
   preserve natural variation but are confounded by overall head
   size.

2. **Proportions**: volume expressed as a proportion of ICV, which
   assumes isometric (1:1) scaling and may over- or under-correct
   depending on the true allometric relationship
   [@de_jong_allometric_2017; @williams_neuroanatomical_2021]:

$$V_{\text{PRP}} = \frac{V}{\text{ICV}} \times 1000$$ {#eq-prp}

3. **Stereotaxic**: volumes in standard template space after
   nonlinear registration, which corrects for global size and
   shape differences:

$$V_{\text{STX}} = V \times |J|$$ {#eq-stx}
where $J$ is the Jacobian determinant of the nonlinear
transformation.

4. **Residualized**: linear regression residuals after removing
   ICV association, with regression coefficients estimated from the
   pooled sample [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020;
   @obrien_statistical_2011]:

$$V_{\text{RES}} = V - \hat{\beta} \times (\text{ICV} - \overline{\text{ICV}})$$ {#eq-res}

Residualization eliminates ICV-related variance and produces more
replicable sex differences compared to proportional methods.

#### HVR Calculation

The hippocampal-to-ventricle ratio (HVR) was computed as:

$$\text{HVR} = \frac{\text{HC}_{\text{total}}}{\text{HC}_{\text{total}} + \text{LV}_{\text{total}}}$$ {#eq-hvr}
where $\text{HC}_{\text{total}}$ and $\text{LV}_{\text{total}}$
denote bilateral sums (left + right) of hippocampal and lateral
ventricular temporal horn volumes, respectively. HVR is bounded between 0 and 1,
with higher values indicating larger hippocampus relative to
ventricles. Because HVR is a ratio of two head-size-dependent
structures, no further head-size adjustment was applied.

### Cognitive Assessment

#### Test Battery

Cognitive data were collected at the imaging visit using the UK
Biobank touchscreen-based cognitive battery [@sudlow_uk_2015],
comprising 12 indicators spanning memory, processing speed,
executive function, and reasoning domains (@tbl-cog-battery).
Timed measures (reaction time, trail making, pair matching
response time) were inverse-coded so that higher scores
consistently indicate better performance across all indicators.
Missing cognitive data were handled using full information maximum
likelihood (FIML) estimation, which uses all available data under
a missing-at-random assumption.

#### Factor Structure: Bifactor CFA

Cognitive indicators were modeled using a bifactor confirmatory
factor analysis (CFA) [@sudlow_uk_2015] with three latent factors.
The general factor (*g*) loaded on all 12 indicators. The
memory-specific factor (Memory~s~, orthogonal to *g*) loaded on
pair matching, numeric memory, and prospective memory. The
processing speed-specific factor (Speed~s~, orthogonal to *g*)
loaded on reaction time, trail making numeric, and symbol digit
substitution correct. Factor scales were set using the marker
variable method (first loading fixed to 1.0 for each factor). All
latent factors were constrained to be orthogonal, consistent with
bifactor model assumptions. Cross-loadings were fixed to zero.
Residual covariances were specified for indicator pairs sharing
method variance within the same test (pair matching time with
errors; symbol digit correct with attempts; trail making numeric
with alphanumeric).

Models were estimated using maximum likelihood with robust
standard errors (MLR) in lavaan [@rosseel_lavaan_2012].

### Statistical Analyses

#### Sex Differences Across Adjustment Methods

##### HVR Self-Normalizing Properties

To evaluate whether HVR reduces head-size confounding, we computed
Pearson correlations between ICV and each brain measure (HC, LV,
HVR) as well as between ICV and each head-size adjusted HC volume
(proportions, stereotaxic, residualized). We expected a
self-normalizing measure to show reduced correlation with ICV
compared to unadjusted volumes.

##### Sex Differences in Brain Measures

Sex differences were quantified using Cohen's d with 95%
confidence intervals [@cohen_statistical_2013], with positive d
indicating females > males by our coding convention. Effect sizes
were computed for all ROI x adjustment method combinations in the
full sample
(N = `r format(n_primary, big.mark=",")`).

To isolate sex effects from head-size confounding, we created an
ICV-matched subsample where females and males were paired on age
($\pm 1$ year) and ICV ($\pm 25$ cc, approximately 0.3 SD).
Matching used the MatchIt package (v4.7.2; @ho_matchit_2011) with
optimal 1:1 matching without replacement
(`method = "optimal"`, `distance = "mahalanobis"`), with calipers
enforcing tolerance bounds. This yielded
N = `r format(n_matched_pairs, big.mark=",")` matched pairs
(total N = `r format(n_matched_pairs * 2, big.mark=",")`). We
reasoned that if sex differences in HC persist after matching on
ICV, they cannot be attributed solely to head-size confounding,
and if HVR shows similar effects in full and matched samples, this
indicates HVR is independent of head size.

#### Age-Related Patterns and Normative Modeling

##### Age x Sex Interactions

Linear regression models tested whether cross-sectional
age-related patterns differed by sex:

$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{\text{Age}} \cdot \text{Age}_i + \beta_{\text{Sex}} \cdot \text{Sex}_i + \beta_{\text{Age} \times \text{Sex}} \cdot \text{Age}_i \times \text{Sex}_i + \varepsilon_i$$ {#eq-age-sex}
where $Y$ is the brain measure, Sex is coded as a binary indicator
(Female = reference), and
$\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. A significant
$\beta_{\text{Age} \times \text{Sex}}$ indicates different age
slopes between sexes. Sex-specific slopes were derived as
$\hat{\beta}_{\text{Age}}$ for females and
$\hat{\beta}_{\text{Age}} + \hat{\beta}_{\text{Age} \times \text{Sex}}$
for males, and their ratio quantified the relative rate of
cross-sectional age-related differences. Separate models were fit
for HC~RES~ and LV~RES~ (both residualized against ICV; @eq-res)
and HVR (self-normalizing; @eq-hvr). Scanner site was not included as a random effect given the low
site ICCs (< 0.05; see Sensitivity Analyses), indicating minimal
site contribution to variance. While age trajectories may be
non-linear (as captured by the GAMLSS normative models below),
linear interaction models were used here to provide interpretable
summary statistics for sex-differential aging rates.

##### Normative Centile Curves

Sex-specific normative centile curves were estimated using
Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape
(GAMLSS) [@rigby_generalized_2005; @bethlehem_brain_2022]. For HC
and LV (unadjusted):

$$\mu = f_\mu(\text{Age}) + \beta_{\text{ICV}} \cdot \text{ICV} + \beta_{\text{Edu}} \cdot \text{Education} + u_{\text{site}}$$ {#eq-gamlss-hc}

For HVR (self-normalizing, no ICV term needed):

$$\mu = f_\mu(\text{Age}) + \beta_{\text{Edu}} \cdot \text{Education} + u_{\text{site}}$$ {#eq-gamlss-hvr}
where $f_\mu(\cdot)$ denotes a cubic spline smooth for the
location parameter and $u_{\text{site}}$ denotes random intercepts
for scanner site. The scale parameter was also modeled as a
function of age, $\sigma = f_\sigma(\text{Age})$, allowing
variance to change across the age range. Model families (Gaussian
and Box-Cox Cole and Green; BCCG) were compared using AIC, with
BIC as secondary criterion. The BCCG distribution was used when
flexible modeling of location ($\mu$), scale ($\sigma$), and
skewness ($\nu$) was warranted; shape parameters beyond $\sigma$
were held constant to maintain parsimony. Centile curves (5th,
10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th, 95th) were generated for ages
45--82 by sex.

Data were split into 80% training and 20% test sets, stratified by
sex and 5-year age bins, to evaluate model fit on independent data
and guard against overfitting. Distribution families were selected
on training data and evaluated on the held-out test set by comparing
observed vs. expected proportions across centiles. Final models
were then fit on the complete cross-sectional sample using the
selected distribution family. Model calibration was additionally
assessed using the longitudinal subsample (N = 2,935; see Data
Source and Participants). Because this subsample comprises the same
participants as the primary cross-sectional sample with an
additional follow-up session, it tests temporal stability rather
than independent validation. Test-retest reliability was quantified
using Pearson correlation and intraclass correlation coefficient
(ICC, two-way random, absolute agreement).

Two sets of GAMLSS models were generated: (1) site-controlled
models including random site intercepts ($u_{\text{site}}$) for
optimal within-UKB accuracy, and (2) transfer models without site
effects for application to external cohorts where site is unknown
or not comparable. Transfer models used identical distribution
families but omitted the random site term, as
site-specific intercepts estimated on UK Biobank
scanners cannot be applied to external cohorts with
different or unknown acquisition sites.

#### Brain-Cognition Associations

Joint measurement-structural equation models tested associations
between brain measures and cognitive factors. These analyses were
restricted to the England subsample
(N = `r format(n_england, big.mark=",")`; see Data Source and
Participants) because the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMDP),
used as a socioeconomic covariate, is not comparable across UK
countries. All models were estimated in R using lavaan
[@rosseel_lavaan_2012].

##### Measurement Invariance

Comparing brain-cognition associations across sexes requires that
the cognitive measurement model is equivalent across groups.
Measurement invariance of the bifactor structure (see Factor
Structure: Bifactor CFA) was therefore tested following standard
multi-group CFA procedures [@putnick_measurement_2016]. Four
nested models were tested: (1) configural invariance (same factor
structure), (2) metric invariance (equal loadings), (3) scalar
invariance (equal intercepts), and (4) strict invariance (equal
residuals). Invariance was evaluated using $\Delta$CFI $\leq$ 0.01
[@cheung_evaluating_2002] and $\Delta$RMSEA $\leq$ 0.015
[@chen_sensitivity_2007]. At minimum, metric invariance is
required to compare structural paths across groups.

##### SEM Specifications

Given adequate measurement invariance, three SEM models were
estimated, each combining the bifactor cognitive measurement model
with structural paths from a brain measure to all three cognitive
factors. Brain measures entered as observed (manifest) variables:
HC (bilateral hippocampal volume, sum of left and right), HVR
(@eq-hvr), and HC~RES~ (HC residualized against ICV within sex,
yielding r $\approx$ 0 with ICV by construction). The structural
component of each model took the following form:

**Model 1 (HC):**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{HC} &= \beta_{\text{Age}} \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_{\text{ICV}} \cdot \text{ICV} + \beta_{\text{Edu}} \cdot \text{Edu} + \beta_{\text{IMDP}} \cdot \text{IMDP} + \zeta_{\text{HC}} \\
\eta_k &= \beta_{k,\text{HC}} \cdot \text{HC} + \beta_{k,\text{Age}} \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_{k,\text{ICV}} \cdot \text{ICV} + \beta_{k,\text{Edu}} \cdot \text{Edu} + \beta_{k,\text{IMDP}} \cdot \text{IMDP} + \zeta_k
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-sem-hc}

**Model 2 (HVR):**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{HVR} &= \beta_{\text{Age}} \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_{\text{Age}^2} \cdot \text{Age}^2 + \beta_{\text{ICV}} \cdot \text{ICV} \\
  &\quad + \beta_{\text{Edu}} \cdot \text{Edu} + \beta_{\text{IMDP}} \cdot \text{IMDP} + \zeta_{\text{HVR}} \\
\eta_k &= \beta_{k,\text{HVR}} \cdot \text{HVR} + \beta_{k,\text{Age}} \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_{k,\text{Age}^2} \cdot \text{Age}^2 \\
  &\quad + \beta_{k,\text{ICV}} \cdot \text{ICV} + \beta_{k,\text{Edu}} \cdot \text{Edu} + \beta_{k,\text{IMDP}} \cdot \text{IMDP} + \zeta_k
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-sem-hvr}

**Model 3 (HC~RES~):**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{HC}_{\text{RES}} &= \beta_{\text{Age}} \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_{\text{Age}^2} \cdot \text{Age}^2 + \beta_{\text{ICV}} \cdot \text{ICV} \\
  &\quad + \beta_{\text{Edu}} \cdot \text{Edu} + \beta_{\text{IMDP}} \cdot \text{IMDP} + \zeta_{\text{HC}_{\text{RES}}} \\
\eta_k &= \beta_{k,\text{HC}_{\text{RES}}} \cdot \text{HC}_{\text{RES}} + \beta_{k,\text{Age}} \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_{k,\text{Age}^2} \cdot \text{Age}^2 \\
  &\quad + \beta_{k,\text{ICV}} \cdot \text{ICV} + \beta_{k,\text{Edu}} \cdot \text{Edu} + \beta_{k,\text{IMDP}} \cdot \text{IMDP} + \zeta_k
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-sem-hcres}

where $\eta_k \in \{g, \text{Memory}_s, \text{Speed}_s\}$ denotes
latent cognitive factors and $\zeta$ denotes residual terms. A
quadratic age term was included in the HVR and HC~RES~ models but
not in the HC model, where the combination of raw hippocampal
volume, ICV, and quadratic age produced multicollinearity. This
difference in model specification means that brain-cognition path
comparisons between HC and the other measures should be interpreted
with this constraint in mind, as the HC model captures only linear
age effects. Age was centered within sex groups before squaring. All structural
variables were z-standardized within sex groups to address scale
differences. Covariates are summarized in
@tbl-sem-covariates-fields.

The HC~RES~ model serves as a benchmark representing the
methodological standard for removing head-size confounding.
Comparing HVR to HC~RES~ tests whether HVR provides similar
cognitive associations while being self-normalizing and capturing
additional variance through its incorporation of ventricular
dynamics. The proportions and stereotaxic adjustment methods were
excluded due to concerns about biologically implausible
associations and residual ICV correlation, respectively
[@wang_comparison_2024].

##### Estimation and Inference

Two estimation approaches were used. Pooled models combined all
participants, included sex as a covariate, and were estimated
using robust maximum likelihood (MLR) with cluster-robust standard
errors to account for scanner site. Multi-group models estimated
separate structural parameters for females and males, allowing sex
differences in brain-cognition paths to be directly tested; these
were estimated using maximum likelihood with bootstrap confidence
intervals (2,000 resamples) [@cumming_inference_2005]. Missing
cognitive data were handled using full information maximum
likelihood (FIML) in both approaches. Sex differences in path
coefficients were evaluated by comparing bootstrap confidence
intervals across groups.

#### Sensitivity Analyses

Three sensitivity analyses assessed the robustness of sex
difference findings to analytical choices.

##### Site effects

Scanner site (UK Biobank assessment centre) can introduce
systematic variance in volumetric measurements due to differences
in scanner hardware, software versions, or acquisition protocols.
Site effects were quantified using the intraclass correlation
coefficient:

$$\text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{site}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{site}} + \sigma^2_{\text{residual}}}$$ {#eq-icc}

Site-adjusted sex difference effect sizes were computed using
linear mixed-effects models with a fixed effect for sex and a
random intercept for scanner site:

$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{\text{Sex}} \cdot \text{Sex}_i + u_{\text{site}(i)} + \varepsilon_i$$ {#eq-site-adj}
where
$u_{\text{site}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\text{site}})$ and
$\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\text{residual}})$.
Cohen's d was approximated as
$\hat{\beta}_{\text{Sex}} / \hat{\sigma}_{\text{residual}}$
[@cohen_statistical_2013], with confidence intervals
derived from the Wald approximation.

##### Hemisphere comparison

Left and right hippocampus and lateral ventricle volumes
(residualized against ICV) were analyzed separately to assess
whether sex differences are lateralized. Cohen's d was computed for
each hemisphere independently, with effect size comparisons based on 95% confidence
intervals. A significant difference in effect magnitude
between hemispheres was inferred when the point estimate
of one hemisphere fell outside the 95% confidence interval
of the other.

##### Inclusion of psychiatric diagnoses

The primary analysis excluded participants with ICD-10 diagnoses
in the F (mental and behavioral disorders), G (neurological), or
Q0 (congenital brain malformations) categories. To assess
robustness, sex difference analyses were repeated in an expanded
sensitivity sample that included participants with F-code
diagnoses (F00-F99) while still excluding G and Q0 codes. The
difference in Cohen's d between primary and sensitivity samples
($\Delta d$ = $d_{\text{primary}}$ - $d_{\text{sensitivity}}$)
quantified the impact of psychiatric exclusion criteria. Small
differences indicate that findings generalize to a less
restrictively selected sample and are not driven by exclusion of
psychiatric comorbidity.

## Results

### Sample Characteristics

The primary sample comprised
`r format(n_primary, big.mark=",")` participants
(`r format(n_female, big.mark=",")` female,
`r format(n_male, big.mark=",")` male; `r pct_female`% female)
aged `r age_min`--`r age_max` years (@tbl-demographics). Females
were slightly younger on average
(M = `r age_mean_f`, SD = `r age_sd_f`) than males
(M = `r age_mean_m`, SD = `r age_sd_m`). Males had substantially
larger ICV than females, consistent with the well-documented sex
difference in head size. The England subsample
(N = `r format(n_england, big.mark=",")`), ICV-matched subsample
(N = `r format(n_matched_pairs * 2, big.mark=",")`;
`r format(n_matched_pairs, big.mark=",")` pairs), and
longitudinal subsample (N = 2,935) showed comparable age and ICV
distributions to the primary sample within their respective
selection constraints.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "**Participant characteristics by sex and sample.** Values are M (SD). d = Cohen's d (Female − Male). England = English assessment centres (SEM analyses). Matched = age $\\pm 1$ yr, ICV $\\pm 25$ cc. Longitudinal = participants with repeat imaging."

lng_demog <- if ("LNG" %in% names(demog_data)) {
  demog_data$LNG
} else {
  NULL
}
format_demographics_gt(
  all_demog, eng_demog, mtch_demog, lng_demog
```

### Sex Differences Across Adjustment Methods

#### HVR Self-Normalizing Properties

Unadjusted HC showed strong positive correlation with ICV
(r = `r round(hvr_icv[VARIABLE == "HC", CORRELATION], 3)`), while
proportions-adjusted HC showed moderate negative correlation
(r = `r round(hvr_icv[VARIABLE == "HC_PRP", CORRELATION], 3)`),
indicating over-correction (@tbl-hvr-validation). Residualization
eliminated ICV association by construction (r $\approx$ 0). HVR's
correlation with ICV
(r = `r round(hvr_icv[VARIABLE == "HVR", CORRELATION], 3)`) was
smaller in magnitude than raw HC
(r = `r round(hvr_icv[VARIABLE == "HC", CORRELATION], 3)`) but
remained negative, unlike residualized HC (r $\approx$ 0). This
represents a
`r round((1 - abs(hvr_icv[VARIABLE == "HVR", CORRELATION]) / abs(hvr_icv[VARIABLE == "HC", CORRELATION])) * 100, 0)`%
reduction in absolute ICV association. The negative direction
mirrors the LV-ICV relationship
(r = `r round(hvr_icv[VARIABLE == "LV", CORRELATION], 3)`),
indicating that the HVR-ICV association reflects the ventricular
component's scaling with head size.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hvr-validation
#| tbl-cap: "**Brain measure correlations with ICV.** An ideal self-normalizing measure shows r(ICV) near zero."

format_hvr_validation_gt(hvr_icv)
```

#### Sex Differences in Brain Measures

Sex differences varied across brain measures and adjustment
methods
(N = `r format(n_primary, big.mark=",")`; @fig-effect-sizes).

##### Hippocampal Volume

HC sex differences reversed direction depending on the adjustment
method. Unadjusted volumes showed
d = `r round(hc_non$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[95% CI: `r round(hc_non$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(hc_non$CI_UPPER, 2)`], indicating males had larger
absolute volumes. Proportions adjustment reversed this to
d = `r round(hc_prp$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[`r round(hc_prp$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(hc_prp$CI_UPPER, 2)`] with females larger. Stereotaxic
adjustment yielded
d = `r round(hc_stx$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[`r round(hc_stx$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(hc_stx$CI_UPPER, 2)`], and residualized volumes showed
a negligible effect
(d = `r round(hc_res$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[`r round(hc_res$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(hc_res$CI_UPPER, 2)`]). The effect size range across
methods spanned
`r round(abs(min(bilateral[ROI == "HC"]$ESTIMATE) - max(bilateral[ROI == "HC"]$ESTIMATE)), 2)`
standard deviations.

##### Lateral Ventricular Volume

Unlike HC, lateral ventricular sex differences were consistently
negative (males > females) across all adjustment methods, though
effect magnitudes were attenuated by head-size correction.
Unadjusted LV showed
d = `r round(lv_non$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[`r round(lv_non$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(lv_non$CI_UPPER, 2)`], similar in magnitude to
unadjusted HC. After adjustment, all methods retained the male
advantage: proportions
d = `r round(lv_prp$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[`r round(lv_prp$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(lv_prp$CI_UPPER, 2)`], stereotaxic
d = `r round(lv_stx$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[`r round(lv_stx$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(lv_stx$CI_UPPER, 2)`], and residualized
d = `r round(lv_res$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[`r round(lv_res$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(lv_res$CI_UPPER, 2)`]. The directional consistency across
methods contrasts with the reversals observed for HC.

##### HVR

HVR showed a consistent female advantage:
d = `r round(hvr_non$ESTIMATE, 2)`
[95% CI: `r round(hvr_non$CI_LOWER, 2)`,
`r round(hvr_non$CI_UPPER, 2)`]. The combination of males having
relatively smaller hippocampi (after head-size adjustment) and
larger ventricles produces this female advantage in HVR.
Distribution overlap between sexes across adjustment methods is
shown in @fig-distributions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-effect-sizes
#| fig-cap: "**Sex differences by adjustment method.** Circles = full sample; triangles = ICV-matched subsample. Faded points indicate non-significant effects (95% confidence interval crosses zero). Right panel shows $\\Delta d$ = $d_{\\text{full}}$ $-$ $d_{\\text{matched}}$, representing the change in effect size after removing head-size confounding; values near zero indicate head-size-independent effects."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| dev: cairo_pdf
fig_effect_sizes_by_adjustment(
  sex_diff, include_matched = TRUE
)
```

##### Matched-Pair Comparison

Matching on age and ICV
(N = `r format(n_matched_pairs * 2, big.mark=",")`;
`r format(n_matched_pairs, big.mark=",")` pairs) revealed which
sex differences persist after removing head-size confounding
(@tbl-matched). HC effects collapsed to near-zero (unadjusted
d = `r round(matched_hc_non$ESTIMATE_MTCH, 2)`), confirming that
HC sex differences are driven by head-size variation. LV effects
were attenuated but remained significant (unadjusted
d = `r round(matched_lv_non$ESTIMATE_MTCH, 2)`), indicating that
males have larger ventricles even at equivalent head size. HVR was
reduced but persisted
(d = `r round(matched_hvr$ESTIMATE_MTCH, 2)`
[`r round(matched_hvr$CI_LOWER_MTCH, 2)`,
`r round(matched_hvr$CI_UPPER_MTCH, 2)`]), consistent with the
female HVR advantage being independent of head-size confounding.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-matched
#| tbl-cap: "**Full vs. ICV-matched subsample effect sizes.** Matching on age ($\\pm 1$ yr) and ICV ($\\pm 25$ cc) eliminates head-size confounding."
if ("COMPARISON" %in% names(sex_diff))
  format_matched_comparison_gt(
    sex_diff$COMPARISON, n_matched_pairs
  )
```

### Age-Related Patterns and Normative Modeling

#### Age x Sex Interactions

Cross-sectional age patterns
(N = `r format(n_primary, big.mark=",")`) differed by sex
(@fig-age-trajectory). For HVR, the age × sex interaction was small but
significant
($\beta$ = `r round(hvr_int$INTERACTION_EST, 4)`,
SE = `r round(hvr_int$INTERACTION_SE, 5)`,
t = `r round(hvr_int$INTERACTION_T, 2)`,
p = `r format(hvr_int$INTERACTION_P, scientific=TRUE, digits=2)`),
with males showing
`r round(abs(hvr_int$SLOPE_RATIO), 2)`x steeper cross-sectional
age-related differences. The female HVR advantage *widened* with
age---effect sizes increased from
d = `r round(hvr_d_young$ESTIMATE, 2)` at ages 45-55 to
d = `r round(hvr_d_old$ESTIMATE, 2)` at ages 75+.

Age x sex interactions were significant for all three measures. HC
showed males with
`r round(abs(hc_int$SLOPE_RATIO), 2)`x steeper cross-sectional
differences
(p = `r format(hc_int$INTERACTION_P, scientific=TRUE, digits=2)`).
LV showed the largest sex disparity, with males exhibiting
`r round(abs(lv_int$SLOPE_RATIO), 2)`x steeper ventricular
expansion
(p = `r format(lv_int$INTERACTION_P, scientific=TRUE, digits=2)`).
The greater sex disparity in ventricular age patterns compared to
hippocampal age patterns explains the intermediate HVR ratio
(`r round(abs(hvr_int$SLOPE_RATIO), 2)`x), as HVR captures both
processes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "**Age-related patterns in sex differences.** Solid line = hippocampal-to-ventricle ratio; dashed lines = hippocampal/ventricular volume. White-filled points = non-significant (95% confidence interval crosses zero)."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig_age_trajectory(sex_diff)
```

#### Normative Centile Curves

@fig-normative-centiles presents sex-specific normative centiles
for HVR, hippocampal volume, and lateral ventricular volume.
Across the age range, females showed higher HVR values at all
percentile levels; the median female HVR at age 55 corresponded
approximately to the 75th percentile for males of the same age.
HC and LV centile curves are generated from GAMLSS models that
include ICV as a covariate, providing head-size adjusted norms
without pre-residualizing the data. Males show greater ventricular
variability at older ages, potentially reflecting greater
heterogeneity in aging patterns.

```{r}
#| label: fig-normative-centiles
#| fig-cap: "**Sex-specific normative centile curves.** Hippocampal-to-ventricle ratio (top), hippocampal volume (middle), and lateral ventricular volume (bottom). Left and right columns show female and male centiles separately; the centre column overlays both sexes for direct comparison. Hippocampal and ventricular volume models include intracranial volume as a covariate."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 7
fig_normative_centiles_panel(norm_tables)
```

Calibration plots (@fig-gamlss-calibration) assess whether
the normative models are well-specified: for each nominal
centile (e.g., the 10th percentile curve), the plot shows
what proportion of observations actually fall below that
curve. A well-calibrated model produces points along the
diagonal (observed proportion = expected proportion). Our
models closely track the diagonal across all centiles,
indicating that the fitted distributions accurately capture
the true variability in the data.

##### Temporal Stability (Longitudinal Validation)

All brain measures demonstrated high test-retest reliability
across the longitudinal follow-up
(@tbl-temporal-stability), with Pearson correlations
> 0.95 and ICCs > 0.93 for all measures. HVR showed slightly
lower reliability
(r = `r round(hvr_r, 3)`, ICC = `r round(hvr_icc, 3)`) compared
to HC
(r = `r round(hc_r, 3)`, ICC = `r round(hc_icc, 3)`) and LV
(r = `r round(lv_r, 3)`, ICC = `r round(lv_icc, 3)`), consistent
with the ratio measure amplifying small measurement errors in
either component. These reliabilities support the use of these
normative models for individual-level assessment.

##### Clinical Normative Centile Tables

Sex-specific normative centile tables for HVR, hippocampal volume,
and lateral ventricular volume are provided in Supporting
Information
(@tbl-hvr-centiles-female--@tbl-lv-centiles-male)
to enable clinical interpretation of individual measurements at
5-year age intervals. These tables allow clinicians to determine
an individual's percentile rank given their age, sex, and brain
measure.

GAMLSS model coefficients for the transfer models (excluding site
random effects) are provided in @tbl-gamlss-hvr-coef and
@tbl-gamlss-hc-coef. These transfer models enable researchers to
compute individual centile scores in external datasets where UK
Biobank site identifiers are not applicable.

### Brain-Cognition Associations

SEM analyses were restricted to the England subsample
(N = `r format(n_england, big.mark=",")`) to ensure comparability
of the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMDP) covariate.

#### Measurement Invariance

The cognitive bifactor model showed acceptable fit at all
invariance levels, with $\Delta$CFI $\leq$ 0.01 and
$\Delta$RMSEA $\leq$ 0.015 at each step
(@tbl-measurement-invariance). Strict measurement
invariance was supported, validating cross-sex comparisons of
factor scores and structural paths.

#### Pooled Model Results

General cognition (*g*) was positively associated with all three
structural brain measures (@tbl-sem-paths): unadjusted HC
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_g$est.std, 3)`
[95% CI: `r safe_round(hc_g$ci.lower, 3)`,
`r safe_round(hc_g$ci.upper, 3)`]), HVR
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hvr_g$est.std, 3)`
[`r safe_round(hvr_g$ci.lower, 3)`,
`r safe_round(hvr_g$ci.upper, 3)`]), and HC~RES~
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_res_g$est.std, 3)`
[`r safe_round(hc_res_g$ci.lower, 3)`,
`r safe_round(hc_res_g$ci.upper, 3)`]), all p < .001. Confidence
intervals overlapped substantially, indicating no significant
differences in predictive validity between measures. HVR showed
numerically the strongest association with *g*, despite requiring
no head-size adjustment.

For processing speed (Speed~s~), HC showed the strongest effect
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_speed$est.std, 3)`, p < .001),
followed by HC~RES~
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_res_speed$est.std, 3)`,
p = `r safe_round(hc_res_speed$pvalue, 3)`), with HVR trending
but not significant
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hvr_speed$est.std, 3)`,
p = `r safe_round(hvr_speed$pvalue, 3)`). The memory-specific
factor (Memory~s~) could not be reliably estimated in either sex
and is therefore not reported here (see
@tbl-sem-loadings for factor loadings).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sem-paths
#| tbl-cap: "**Pooled brain-cognition path coefficients.** Beta = standardized path coefficient; CI from 2000 bootstrap resamples. Memory-specific factor paths not shown due to factor collapse."

format_pooled_sem_paths_gt(
  sem_params, hvr_g, hc_res_g, hc_g
)
```

#### Sex-Stratified Results

@fig-sem-forest displays sex-stratified path coefficients from
multi-group models
(@tbl-sem-paths-by-sex). The multigroup analyses revealed
sex differences in brain-cognition associations.

For general cognition (*g*), HC~RES~ -> *g* was not significant in
males
(p = `r safe_round(hc_res_g_m$pvalue, 3)`) while remaining
significant in females. In contrast, HVR showed the opposite
pattern: males exhibited stronger HVR-cognition associations
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hvr_g_m$est.std, 3)`) than females
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hvr_g_f$est.std, 3)`), with both
significant. For processing speed (Speed~s~), males showed
significant HC and HC~RES~ associations
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_speed_m$est.std, 3)` and
`r safe_round(hc_res_speed_m$est.std, 3)`, respectively) while
females showed none, suggesting sex-differential neural substrates
for processing speed performance. Neither sex showed significant
HVR -> Speed~s~ associations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sem-forest
#| fig-cap: "**Brain-cognition paths by sex.** Points represent standardized coefficients; lines show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. White-filled points indicate non-significant effects."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
fig_sem_forest(sem_params)
```

All SEM models demonstrated good fit according to conventional
criteria (@tbl-sem-fit; @hu_cutoff_1999). Full model
parameters including factor loadings and covariate effects are
reported in @tbl-sem-loadings and
@tbl-sem-covariate-effects.

##### Non-Linear Age Effects

As described in Methods, quadratic age terms were included
in HVR and HC~RES~ models but not in the HC model due to
multicollinearity; fit indices for the HC model
(@tbl-sem-fit) therefore reflect a linear-age
specification. All quadratic age effects were significantly
negative (all p < .001; @tbl-sem-covariate-effects),
indicating that cross-sectional differences between older
and younger participants were disproportionately larger at
older ages. HVR showed a stronger quadratic effect
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hvr_age_sq$est.std, 3)`) than
HC~RES~
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_res_age_sq$est.std, 3)`),
consistent with HVR capturing both hippocampal and
ventricular age-related changes, both of which accelerate
at older ages. Cognitive factors showed comparable quadratic
effects across models (*g*:
$\beta$ $\approx$ `r safe_round(g_age_sq_hvr$est.std, 3)`;
Speed~s~:
$\beta$ $\approx$ `r safe_round(speed_age_sq_hvr$est.std, 3)`).

### Sensitivity Analyses

#### Site-Adjusted Effect Sizes

Site ICCs ranged from 0.004 to 0.012
(@tbl-site-adjusted), indicating that scanner site
explained less than 1.5% of total variance in all brain measures.
Effect sizes remained consistent after site adjustment.

#### Hemisphere Comparison

Sex difference effect sizes were largely symmetrical across
hemispheres for the individual volumes
(@tbl-hemisphere, @fig-hemisphere). Residualized
hippocampal volume showed significant effects bilaterally
(left d = -0.14, right d = -0.16), with each point
estimate falling within the other's confidence interval,
indicating no lateralized sex difference. Lateral
ventricles similarly showed a male advantage in both hemispheres
with nearly identical effect sizes
(left d = 0.48, right d = 0.48). However, HVR showed a
lateralized pattern: the right hemisphere exhibited a significant
female advantage (d = 0.05 [0.03, 0.07]), while the left
hemisphere effect was non-significant
(d = -0.01 [-0.03, 0.02]).

#### Inclusion of Psychiatric Diagnoses (F-Codes)

Effect sizes remained stable when including participants with
psychiatric diagnoses (N = 30,032;
@tbl-sensitivity, @fig-sensitivity),
demonstrating robustness of findings to exclusion criteria.

## Discussion

### Summary of Findings

In `r format(n_primary, big.mark=",")` UK Biobank participants, we
evaluated HVR as a self-normalizing biomarker that bypasses
conventional head-size correction. HVR showed weak correlation with
ICV, substantially reducing head-size dependence compared to
unadjusted HC. Hippocampal sex differences ranged from
d = `r round(hc_non$ESTIMATE, 2)` (males larger) to
d = `r round(hc_prp$ESTIMATE, 2)` (females larger) depending
solely on the adjustment method and age, whereas HVR consistently showed a
female advantage replicated in the ICV-matched subsample. Males
showed steeper age-related HVR differences
(`r round(abs(hvr_int$SLOPE_RATIO), 2)`x female slope), with the
female advantage widening at older ages
(d = `r round(hvr_d_young$ESTIMATE, 2)` at 45-55y to
d = `r round(hvr_d_old$ESTIMATE, 2)` at 75+y). HVR predicted
general cognition comparably to hippocampal volume.

### Sex Differences Across Adjustment Methods

HVR achieves head-size independence through its mathematical
construction: both numerator (HC) and denominator (HC + LV) scale
with head size, so their ratio largely normalizes out this
confound. @schoemaker2019 demonstrated that HVR yielded stronger
correlations with both age and memory performance than absolute
hippocampal volume, supporting its utility as an integrity index.
In the present sample, HVR achieved a
`r icv_reduction_pct`% reduction in ICV correlation compared to
unadjusted HC
(r = `r round(r_hvr_icv, 3)` vs. r = `r round(r_hc_icv, 3)`).
This approach complements other ratio measures in clinical
neuroimaging, such as the Evans' index
[@curra_ventricular_2019], and avoids the pitfalls of proportional
ICV correction when brain structures scale non-isometrically with
head size [@wang_comparison_2024; @pintzka_marked_2015]. The
residual negative HVR-ICV correlation likely reflects ventricular
scaling: the hippocampus scales hypoallometrically with ICV while
lateral ventricles scale near-isometrically
[@de_jong_allometric_2017], so larger heads have
disproportionately larger ventricles relative to hippocampal
volume, naturally producing lower HVR. Unlike residualization,
which removes all ICV association by construction, HVR preserves
morphological variation related to how ventricular space scales
with brain size.

The reversal of HC sex differences across adjustment
methods---from d = `r round(hc_non$ESTIMATE, 2)` (males larger,
unadjusted) to d = `r round(hc_prp$ESTIMATE, 2)` (females larger,
proportions-adjusted), a swing of `r round(abs(hc_d_range), 2)`
SD---indicates these differences reflect head-size confounding
rather than biology. This over-correction arises because the
hippocampus scales hypoallometrically with ICV ($\alpha$ = 0.60;
@de_jong_allometric_2017), so dividing by ICV systematically
overestimates relative volume in smaller heads
[@pintzka_marked_2015; @voevodskaya_effects_2014]. The pattern
replicates across multiple cohorts
[@pintzka_marked_2015; @voevodskaya_effects_2014;
@fjell_minute_2009], and @ritchie_sex_2018 reported that
unadjusted hippocampal sex differences in the UK Biobank dropped
to near-zero after regression-based adjustment. The near-zero
residualized effect
(d = `r round(hc_res$ESTIMATE, 3)`) suggests no meaningful sex
difference after appropriate statistical control. While total
hippocampal volume sex differences appear methodologically
determined, sex-specific trajectories in hippocampal subregions
[@mu_effect_2020] and structural connectivity patterns
[@ingalhalikar_sex_2014] suggest meaningful differences may exist
at finer spatial scales. Lateral ventricles, by contrast, showed a
consistent male advantage across all methods
(@fig-effect-sizes). Because the LV-ICV regression has a negative
y-intercept, proportional correction under-corrects rather than
over-corrects ventricular volumes---the opposite of what occurs for
HC [@pintzka_marked_2015]. The male advantage persists or increases
after correction [@fjell_minute_2009], and in our large sample,
residualized LV differences remained significant
(d = `r round(lv_res$ESTIMATE, 2)`), suggesting that null findings
in smaller studies may reflect insufficient power. The consistent
male ventricular advantage contrasts sharply with the
method-dependent HC reversals, indicating this sex difference is
not a head-size artifact.

The matched-pair analysis (@tbl-matched) provides the strongest
test of head-size independence. Matching on age and ICV eliminates
head-size variation without the mathematical assumptions of
statistical correction
[@brzezinski-rittner_disentangling_2025]. When matched, the HC sex
difference collapsed to
d = `r round(matched_hc_non$ESTIMATE_MTCH, 3)` (effectively
zero), replicating prior matched-sample findings
[@pintzka_marked_2015; @voevodskaya_effects_2014], while LV
retained a male advantage
(d = `r round(matched_lv_non$ESTIMATE_MTCH, 2)`) and HVR retained
a significant female advantage
(d = `r round(matched_hvr$ESTIMATE_MTCH, 3)`). The HVR effect
decreased `r hvr_reduction_pct`% from full to matched samples,
indicating that most of the sex difference is attributable to
head-size variation, but a significant residual persists. Since
HVR = HC/(HC+LV), the female advantage arises from two converging
factors: comparable hippocampal volumes after size matching and
relatively smaller female ventricles. This
convergence---HC collapsing while LV and HVR effects survive ICV
matching---confirms that the female HVR advantage reflects genuine
sex differences in the hippocampus-to-ventricle balance, not
head-size confounding.

### Age-Related Patterns and Normative Modeling

Males showed steeper cross-sectional differences across all
measures: `r round(hvr_int$SLOPE_RATIO, 2)`x for HVR
(p = `r format(hvr_int$INTERACTION_P, scientific=TRUE, digits=2)`),
`r round(hc_int$SLOPE_RATIO, 2)`x for HC, and
`r round(lv_int$SLOPE_RATIO, 2)`x for LV, consistent with steeper
male subcortical decline reported by @ritchie_sex_2018 and steeper
male CSF expansion by @fjell_minute_2009. The greater sex disparity
in ventricular differences
(`r round(lv_int$SLOPE_RATIO, 2)`x) compared to hippocampal
differences (`r round(hc_int$SLOPE_RATIO, 2)`x) explains HVR's
intermediate ratio: HVR captures both processes, and steeper male
ventricular expansion amplifies hippocampal differences. Males also
show earlier ventricular abnormality signatures, with ventricular
enlargement accelerating in the seventies
[@curra_ventricular_2019], consistent with the steeper male HVR
differences observed here. While the cross-sectional design
precludes identifying a specific onset age, our age-stratified
effect sizes show the male-female HVR divergence is already
present in the youngest bin (ages 45--55,
d = `r round(hvr_d_young$ESTIMATE, 2)`) and widens
monotonically with age
(d = `r round(hvr_d_old$ESTIMATE, 2)` at ages 75+),
suggesting the divergence begins before midlife. However,
@brzezinski-rittner_disentangling_2025 found that hippocampal
age x sex interactions disappeared in a TIV-matched subsample,
suggesting that some sex-differential aging trajectories may be
byproducts of initial brain size differences.

The prognostic relevance of age-pattern differences is supported
by
evidence that steeper hippocampal volume loss predicts dementia
conversion [@rajagopal_estimating_2024]. Cumulative estrogen
exposure may contribute to the female advantage, as longer
reproductive spans are associated with younger brain ages
[@luders_case_2025] and estrogen promotes hippocampal neurogenesis
and synaptic plasticity [@jett_endogenous_2022]. However, the
female advantage is not universal: female APOE e4 carriers show
faster hippocampal loss than male carriers in aMCI
[@park_sex-specific_2025], indicating that genetic risk can
modulate typical sex-differential patterns. Other large studies
have found no significant sex differences in hippocampal age slopes
[@fjell_minute_2009; @pintzka_marked_2015], underscoring that the
presence of age x sex interactions depends on sample size, age
range, and head-size adjustment method. These cross-sectional
patterns cannot establish true individual trajectories and may be
confounded by cohort effects or differential survival; longitudinal
validation is essential.

The sex-specific centile curves (@fig-normative-centiles) extend
normative brain charts
[@bethlehem_brain_2022; @dima_subcortical_2022;
@ge_normative_2024] by providing the first sex-specific reference
values for HVR. Our GAMLSS approach aligns with
@bethlehem_brain_2022 and @dima_subcortical_2022, flexibly modeling
both non-linear age trends and age-related variability changes.
Sex-specific norms are essential to avoid misclassification,
consistent with recommendations from
@williams_neuroanatomical_2021 and @ge_normative_2024, who found
that sex accounts for a considerable proportion of morphological
variance. For residualized HC, sex differences in centiles are
minimal, consistent with the near-zero Cohen's d for residualized
volumes, supporting combined norms when proper ICV adjustment is
applied. For LV, males show greater ventricular variability at
older ages, potentially reflecting greater heterogeneity in
aging-related patterns. Well-calibrated centile estimates
(@fig-gamlss-calibration) have demonstrated clinical utility in
detecting case-control differences and predicting diagnostic
transition from MCI to Alzheimer's disease
[@bethlehem_brain_2022; @dima_subcortical_2022].
HVR showed slightly lower test-retest reliability
(ICC > 0.93; @tbl-temporal-stability) than HC or LV alone
over a mean 2.7-year follow-up. Because this interval
spans real aging-related change, the lower ICC may partly
reflect HVR's sensitivity to concurrent hippocampal
atrophy and ventricular expansion rather than measurement
noise alone — a hypothesis that dedicated longitudinal
studies with shorter retest intervals could directly test.

### Brain-Cognition Associations

Strict measurement invariance for the cognitive bifactor model
($\Delta$CFI $\leq$ 0.01 and $\Delta$RMSEA $\leq$ 0.015 at each
level; @tbl-measurement-invariance) confirmed that the same
cognitive constructs (*g*, Memory~s~, Speed~s~) exist in both sexes
with equivalent loadings, intercepts, and residual variances
[@chen_sensitivity_2007; @putnick_measurement_2016], validating
cross-sex comparison of brain-cognition paths. In pooled models,
HVR predicted general cognition comparably to HC without requiring
head-size adjustment (HVR -> *g*
$\beta$ = `r safe_round(hvr_g$est.std, 3)` vs.
HC -> *g*
$\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_g$est.std, 3)`, overlapping CIs), with
all effects small---consistent with the modest brain-cognition
associations typically observed in large healthy samples
[@ritchie_sex_2018; @wang_comparison_2024]. The restricted
cognitive range in healthy volunteer samples likely attenuates
these associations [@bachmann_age-_2023]. Multigroup analyses
revealed sex-differential patterns: HC~RES~ predicted cognition in
females but not males
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_res_g_m$est.std, 3)`,
p = `r safe_round(hc_res_g_m$pvalue, 3)`), consistent with
stronger female hippocampal-cognition associations reported
elsewhere [@zheng_sex_2017; @jockwitz_differential_2024]. Raw HC
showed significant associations in both sexes but with a female
advantage
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_g_f$est.std, 3)` vs.
`r safe_round(hc_g_m$est.std, 3)`). HVR showed the opposite
pattern, with males exhibiting stronger associations
($\beta$ = `r safe_round(hvr_g_m$est.std, 3)` vs.
`r safe_round(hvr_g_f$est.std, 3)`), though both sexes reached
significance.

These sex-differential patterns indicate that HVR is not simply
"residualized HC by another means." Unlike HC~RES~, which lost
predictive validity in males, HVR maintained significant
associations in both sexes---paralleling
@schoemaker2019 and
@fernandez-lozano_enhanced_2025, who found that HVR predicted
cognition comparably or better than HC alone. The differential
patterns between HC~RES~ and HVR across sexes suggest HVR captures
distinct information related to hippocampus-ventricle coupling. HVR
also accommodated quadratic age specifications that raw HC could
not (the HC + ICV + age^2^ combination produced
multicollinearity), allowing detection of accelerating age-related
patterns ($\beta$~age²~ = `r safe_round(hvr_age_sq$est.std, 3)`
for HVR vs. `r safe_round(hc_res_age_sq$est.std, 3)` for
HC~RES~). The stronger quadratic effect for HVR reflects its
capture of both hippocampal and ventricular age-related
differences. The ventricular component likely contributes
cognitive-relevant variance beyond medial temporal integrity, as
total lateral ventricular volume has been associated with
executive function rather than episodic memory
[@bachmann_age-_2023], though this finding pertains to total
lateral ventricles rather than the temporal horns measured
here.

### Sensitivity Analyses

Low site ICCs (all < 0.05; @tbl-site-adjusted) confirmed minimal
scanner site contribution to variance, and effect sizes were stable
after site adjustment; the ratio construction of HVR did not
amplify site-related noise. Sex difference effect sizes were
symmetrical across hemispheres for HC and LV; HVR showed a small
lateralized pattern (right d = 0.05 vs. left d = -0.01), though
the small magnitude and potential contribution of hemispheric
segmentation biases [@fernandez-lozano_enhanced_2025] suggest
bilateral HVR remains most robust for clinical application.
Including participants with psychiatric diagnoses changed effect
sizes minimally
($\Delta$d < 0.02; @tbl-sensitivity, @fig-sensitivity), consistent
with the low prevalence of psychiatric diagnoses in this healthy
volunteer cohort [@fry_comparison_2017].

### Limitations

Design and sample constraints include the cross-sectional design,
which cannot distinguish age effects from cohort effects or
establish individual change trajectories, and HVR's conflation of
hippocampal and ventricular contributions to observed differences.
UK Biobank participants are healthier and more educated than the
general population [@fry_comparison_2017], limiting
generalizability to clinical populations. Some cognitive tests had
incomplete data, and complete-case analyses may introduce selection
bias. APOE genotype was unavailable, precluding examination of
gene x sex interactions relevant to dementia risk.

Methodologically, the study did not include power-corrected
proportions allometric adjustment [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020].
Imaging site clustering was not modeled in multigroup SEM because
lavaan does not support this combination
[@rosseel_lavaan_2012], though the minimal design effect across 4
sites makes sex comparisons conservative rather than biased. The
bifactor model's memory-specific factor could not be reliably
estimated in either sex---a common occurrence in bifactor models
[@eid_anomalous_2017; @burns_application_2020]---indicating that
memory variance was fully captured by *g*; brain-cognition paths
involving Memory~s~ are therefore not reported. Ratios can exhibit
non-normality and complex interpretation when numerator and
denominator correlate differently with outcomes, though HVR showed
approximately normal distributions here. All brain-cognition
associations were small ($\beta$ = 0.02--0.04), explaining less
than 1% of variance in cognitive performance. While statistically
significant given the large sample, the practical and clinical
significance of these associations remains to be established.

### Future Directions

The current findings motivate four lines of follow-up work. First,
the UK Biobank repeat imaging subsample enables longitudinal
validation of whether HVR predicts individual-level cognitive
decline. Second, clinical validation in AD/MCI cohorts would
assess HVR's diagnostic utility compared to clinical populations
studied previously [@fernandez-lozano_enhanced_2025]. Third,
longitudinal data could separate hippocampal and ventricular
contributions to HVR changes, which the cross-sectional ratio
conflates. Fourth, examining whether
HVR x sex x APOE genotype predicts dementia conversion would
address the gene x sex interactions that this study could not
explore.

### Conclusions

In `r format(n_primary, big.mark=",")` UK Biobank participants
(`r pct_female`% female), hippocampal sex differences reversed
direction across adjustment methods
(d range: `r round(abs(hc_d_range), 1)` SD), confirming their
methodological determination. HVR demonstrated substantial
head-size independence
(r~ICV~ = `r round(r_hvr_icv, 2)`;
`r icv_reduction_pct`% reduction vs. raw HC) and a consistent
female advantage replicated in the ICV-matched subsample
(d = `r round(matched_hvr$ESTIMATE_MTCH, 2)`). Males showed
`r round(hvr_int$SLOPE_RATIO, 2)`x steeper age-related HVR
differences
(p = `r format(hvr_int$INTERACTION_P, scientific=TRUE, digits=2)`);
sex-specific normative centile curves are provided for research
application, pending validation in clinical populations. HVR
predicted general cognition comparably to hippocampal volume
(HVR -> *g*:
$\beta$ = `r safe_round(hvr_g$est.std, 3)` vs.
HC -> *g*:
$\beta$ = `r safe_round(hc_g$est.std, 3)`, overlapping CIs),
maintained predictive validity in both sexes while residualized HC
lost significance in males
(p = `r safe_round(hc_res_g_m$pvalue, 3)`), and supported more
complex SEM specifications that raw HC could not.
